segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Saul approved of his killing. On that day a great persecution broke out against the assembly in Jerusalem, and all except the apostles were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Devout men buried Stephen and made a great lamentation over him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Saul was ravaging the assembly; going into house after house, he dragged off both men and women and handed them over to prison.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, those who had been scattered went from place to place announcing the good news of the word.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed the Messiah to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The crowds with one mind paid attention to what Philip said, as they listened and saw the signs he was doing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For unclean spirits, shouting with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And there was great joy in that city.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now a man named Simon had already been in the city practicing magic and amazing the people of Samaria, claiming to be someone great.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This man is the Power of God that is called Great.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when they believed Philip as he announced the good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Simon himself also believed, and after he was baptized he stayed close to Philip; and seeing signs and great deeds of power taking place, he was amazed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who went down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for the Spirit had not yet fallen on any of them; they had only been baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Give me this authority too, so that anyone I lay my hands on may receive the Holy Spirit.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Peter said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “May your silver go to destruction along with you, because you thought you could acquire the gift of God with money!

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: You have neither part nor share in this matter, for your heart is not straight before God.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So turn back from this wickedness of yours, and plead with the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of wrongdoing.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Simon answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You plead with the Lord for me, so that nothing of what you have said may come upon me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, after they had solemnly testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they started back to Jerusalem, and they announced the good news to many villages of the Samaritans.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: An angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Get up and go toward the south, to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This is a desert road.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he got up and went. And there was an Ethiopian man, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasury. He had come to Jerusalem to worship,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and was returning, sitting in his chariot and reading the prophet Isaiah.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Spirit said to Philip,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “Go over and join this chariot.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Philip ran up and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet, and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do you really understand what you are reading?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “How could I, unless someone guides me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The passage of scripture he was reading was this:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer, so he does not open his mouth.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: In his humiliation justice was taken from him. Who will describe his generation? For his life is taken from the earth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The eunuch responded to Philip,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I beg you, who is the prophet saying this about? Himself, or someone else?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Philip opened his mouth and, beginning from this scripture, announced to him the good news about Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they were going along the road, they came to some water, and the eunuch said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, water! What prevents me from being baptized?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He ordered the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, for he went on his way rejoicing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through he announced the good news to all the cities until he came to Caesarea.

notes.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint's word for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

notes.phrase: announcing the good news of the word
notes.note: The verb means to bring or announce good news, and here 'the word' is its direct object: the message is what is announced as good news. Most translations use 'preach' or 'preach the gospel', which now sound like church activities. The same verb recurs in verses 12, 25, 35 and 40.

With the article and without the name Jesus, the Greek word is a title here: the anointed king Israel expected. The Samaritans had their own hope of a coming figure. Several modern translations likewise use 'Messiah' where the title is the point and keep 'Christ' where it works as a name, as in verse 12.

Important early manuscripts read 'the city of Samaria'; many others omit the article, giving 'a city of Samaria'. With the article the phrase probably means the region's chief city, though which city Luke has in mind is uncertain. The ancient city of Samaria had been rebuilt by Herod as Sebaste.

notes.phrase: the Power of God that is called Great
notes.note: The crowd's acclamation treats Simon as the embodiment or representative of the supreme divine power, and 'the Great Power' appears to be a recognised title. Its exact background, Samaritan or more broadly Hellenistic, is uncertain. Later Christian writers made Simon the founder of a sect, but those accounts may not reflect what Luke knew.

The Greek is the plural of the word 'power' used in verse 10, with the same adjective 'great'. The man acclaimed as the Great Power is himself amazed, the verb used of his effect on others in verses 9 and 11, at great powers at work through Philip. 'Miracles' is the common rendering and correct in sense, but it hides the echo.

The Greek word is the one translated 'word' in verses 4, 14 and 25, and it can also mean 'matter' or 'affair'. Peter may mean that Simon has no share in the matter at hand, the giving of the Spirit, or that he has no share in the message itself. Most translations take the first sense, as here.

The Greek verb carries the prophets' call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct, here explicitly 'from' wickedness. Most translations keep 'repent', understood as including a change of life. In current English that word centres on feeling sorry, which is narrower than the Greek.

notes.phrase: in the gall of bitterness and the bond of wrongdoing
notes.note: Peter's language echoes the Greek Old Testament. 'Gall and bitterness' recalls the warning in Deuteronomy 29 against a person whose heart turns away from God to idolatry, and 'bond of wrongdoing' is a phrase from Isaiah 58:6. The sense is that Simon is steeped in a poisonous bitterness and held captive by wrongdoing.

The Greek word means 'midday' and, by extension, 'the south'. The phrase can therefore be read as 'at about noon' instead of 'toward the south'. Most translations choose the direction, which suits a road running from Jerusalem to Gaza, but the time reading is grammatically possible and has scholarly support.

The Greek says only 'this is desert', meaning uninhabited country. It may describe the road or the city of Gaza, whose old site lay deserted. It may also be part of the angel's words and not, as taken here, a comment by the narrator.

'Candace' (Kandake) was not a personal name but the title borne by the ruling queens or queen mothers of the kingdom of Meroe. 'Ethiopia' in ancient usage meant that kingdom, on the Nile south of Egypt in what is now Sudan, and not the modern country. To Greek and Roman readers it stood for the far southern edge of the known world.

The quotation follows the Greek version of Isaiah 53:7–8, which differs from the Hebrew. Literally 'his judgment was taken away', the line may mean he was denied a fair judgment, as most translations take it, or that the sentence against him was lifted. The next line, 'who will describe his generation?', is also obscure and may refer to his descendants, his contemporaries or his origin.

notes.phrase: What prevents me from being baptized?
notes.note: Verse 37 is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts and is not printed in the Greek text translated here. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add Philip's reply, 'If you believe with all your heart, you may,' and the eunuch's confession, 'I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.' It is generally regarded as an early addition, perhaps reflecting baptismal practice.

candidates.reason: Recurs across the Gospels, Acts and the letters and varies in English between 'preach' and 'proclaim'; it needs one rendering that is kept distinct from εὐαγγελίζω.
The plural is traditionally 'miracles' but is the same word as 'power'; a consistent policy is needed so that echoes like Acts 8:10 and 8:13 survive across books.
Ranges from bowing before a superior to worship of God; translators vary between 'worship', 'bow down' and 'pay homage', and the choice carries theological weight in the Gospels and Revelation.
Often rendered 'power' as well as 'authority', which blurs it with δύναμις; one decision would keep the two words distinct throughout.
Rendered variously as 'destruction', 'perdition', 'ruin' or 'perish' across the New Testament; readers draw conclusions about final judgment from the English chosen.

warnings: Verse 4: εὐαγγελίζω is not rendered with a register form (announce the good news) and has no register-exception note.
Verse 35: εὐαγγελίζω is not rendered with a register form (announce the good news) and has no register-exception note.
